cards.text: King Solomon is ruling over Israel, and the text starts with his chief officials: priests, secretaries, a recorder, a palace manager, a man over the forced labor and Benaiah son of Jehoiada in charge of the army. That's a LOT of job titles. On my cookie planet I'm every single one of them, and I STILL show up late.

Next come twelve governors over all Israel, region by region, and each one provides food for the king and his household for one month of the year. Two of them are married to Solomon's daughters. I bet those two NEVER miss their month.
Now step back and look at the people of Judah and Israel. There are a whole lot of them, and let's just say it's a good time to live there.

cards.question: What picture does the writer use for how many people of Judah and Israel there are?

answers.text: As numerous as the sand on the seashore
As numerous as the stars in the sky
As numerous as the dust of the earth

cards.question: All those people of Judah and Israel are eating and drinking and rejoicing.

cards.text: And Solomon's reign stretches WAY past Israel. He reigns over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines, all the way to the border of Egypt.

cards.question: The kingdoms under Solomon rebel against him every chance they get.

cards.text: Then the text lists Solomon's provisions for a single day: thirty cors of fine flour, sixty cors of meal, ten fat oxen, twenty range oxen and a hundred sheep, plus deer, gazelles, roebucks and fattened poultry. ONE day. I bake every single morning, friend, and I have never once needed a cor of anything.

cards.question: Solomon has dominion over everything west of the Euphrates, from Tiphsah to Gaza. And he has ___ on all sides.
Throughout Solomon's days, Judah and Israel dwell securely from Dan to Beersheba. What picture does the writer use for each man?

answers.text: Under his own vine and fig tree

cards.text: Solomon also has 4,000 stalls for his chariot horses and 12,000 horses. Each month the governors take their turn, bringing food for the king's table and barley and straw for all those horses. Twelve THOUSAND horses, friend. I can't keep track of ONE timer.

cards.question: The governors see to it that nothing is lacking for King Solomon and all who come to his table.

cards.text: Now here's the part I love. God gives Solomon wisdom, exceedingly deep insight and understanding beyond measure.

cards.question: That picture again! Solomon's understanding is beyond measure, like the ___ on the seashore.
Solomon's wisdom is greater than that of all the men of the East, and greater than all the wisdom of ___.

cards.text: He's wiser than all men, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and wiser than Heman, Calcol and Darda, the sons of Mahol. I once got swapped out for a shiny new stamper, so I think I know EXACTLY how Darda feels.

cards.question: Solomon's fame stays inside Israel's borders.
Solomon's songs number a thousand and five. How many proverbs does he compose?
Solomon speaks of trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop growing in the wall. What else does he teach about?

answers.text: Animals and birds and reptiles and fish
The stars and the moon and the seasons

cards.question: All the kings of the earth hear about Solomon's wisdom. What do they do?

answers.text: Send men to listen to him
Ban his words in their lands

findings.problem: The setup line 'let's just say it's a good time to live there' gives away the answer to card 5, which asks whether the people are eating, drinking and rejoicing. It also leans toward card 9's answer of 'peace'.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences. It isn't a long-stretch summary, because card 12 asks about verse 27 from inside its range.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The wrong answers 'Babylon' and 'Assyria' are both lands to the east. The same verse says Solomon's wisdom was greater than that of all the men of the East, so a baker could argue that either one is also right.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: Choosing three thousand proverbs over three hundred or thirteen hundred is pure luck. Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason toward the number. This stop already has several discovery questions (cards 4, 10, 15 and 19).

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: Sand, stars and dust are all biblical pictures for a huge number, and nothing on card 3 points to one over the others. The pick comes down to luck.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: Cards 2 and 8 are long-stretch summaries (4:7-19 and 4:22-23), and each runs three sentences once the joke is included. The bite-sized rule says every non-opening story card is 1 to 2 sentences. The good genealogy example under 'Long stretches' is four sentences.
findings.question: Are long-stretch summary story cards held to the 1 to 2 sentence limit, or may they run longer, as in the Genesis 5 example?
